BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS

Proposal for Decision

The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) audited ************** (Petitioner) for compliance with mixed beverage tax laws and sales tax laws and made three assessments: one for mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT), one for mixed beverage sales tax (MBST), and one for sales and use tax. Each assessment included tax, 10% late penalty, and accrued interest. The MBST and MBGRT assessments also included a 50% fraud penalty. Petitioner requested redetermination for each hearing. Petitioner raised no specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment but disagreed with the audit methodology and contended general audit error for the MBST and MBGRT assessments. In this Proposal for Decision (PFD), the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) finds that the assessments, including the 50% fraud penalties, should be upheld.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on June 15, 2023, issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. On June 16, 2023, ALJ Kathy Pickup issued an order setting the written submission hearing and combining the cases for purposes of issuing a single PFD. Petitioner subsequently filed an agreed motion to convert to an in-person hearing, which was granted. Janice Cahalane represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by its managing member, **************. The hearing convened on November 29, 2023. The record closed on December 1, 2023, after the parties filed the evidence that was admitted at the hearing.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction in this proceeding. Therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner submitted sales reports and complimentary drink reports for January 1, 2019, through March 15, 2022.

Staff presented the testimony of the auditor, INDIVIDUAL and submitted the following exhibits for each hearing:

1. Hearing Request Receipt Letters;

2. Texas Notifications of Audit Results;

3. Penalty and Interest Waiver Worksheets;

4. Audit Package (MBGRT);

5. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (MBGRT);

6. Audit Package (MBST);

7. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (MBST);

8. Audit Package (Sales and Use Tax);

9. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (Sales and Use Tax);

10. Audit Referral Report for Additional Penalty (Mixed Beverage Taxes);

11. Posts from Petitioner’s Facebook Page;

12. Posts from Petitioner’s Facebook Page for Periods from November 2020 to September 2021; and

13. Vendor-Reported Purchase Data Summay for the Tax Period.

The parties’ exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. AGREED ADJUSTMENTS

Staff did not agree to amend any of the assessments.

C. MATERIAL FACTS

During the period at issue, Petitioner held a mixed beverage permit and a sales and use tax permit, and operated a sports bar, COMPANY, in CITY, Texas. The bar also sold food items.

In August 2021, Staff initiated a MBGRT, MBST, and sales tax audit of Petitioner for the period January 1, 2018, through September 30, 2021. At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit. Petitioner did not provide any records.

A depletion analysis was performed based on the average serving size for distilled spirits and beer and vendor-reported purchases. The auditor conducted a pour test on August 26, 2021. During the pour observation, the auditor tested five drinks, which resulted in an average pour of 1.41 ounces for distilled spirits and 14.88 ounces for beer.[4] Using the serving sizes and Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and beer available for sale during the audit period. Due to the lack of documentation provided by Petitioner, the auditor used prices obtained from the pour test observation to determine the average selling price, then multiplied those prices by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer. Petitioner did not provide the auditor with documentation of complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, theft, breakage, or other potential allowances.

The differences between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for each beverage category. The auditor applied the respective underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from sales of distilled spirits and beer for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

On March 14, 2022, Staff issued Texas Notifications of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing liabilities for MBGRT and MBST. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for sales and use tax. All assessments included tax, a 10% penalty, and accrued interest. The MBGRT and MBST assessments also included a 50% additional penalty. The overall error rate in reporting tax was 65.41% for MBST and 64.66% for MBGRT. Petitioner had 37 late returns during the audit period for MBGRT and 36 late returns for MBST.

Petitioner requested redetermination, disagreeing with the audit methodology used and contending general audit error for the MBST and MBGRT assessments. Petitioner did not provide any records and did not raise any specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment. Staff contends no adjustments are warranted and referred the matters to SOAH.

D. ALJ’S ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. “Taxable items” include tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010. The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

In addition to the sales tax due on taxable items, a 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001. In addition, an 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

As a mixed beverage permit holder, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4). In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the gross receipts tax and sales tax liability based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. Id. §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. Id. Thus, mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See id.; Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017). The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011). Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation.[5] Mixed beverage audits performed in accordance with proper auditing practices and procedures, based upon the best information available, are presumed to be correct. Comptroller’s Decision No. 41,997 (2004).

Petitioner states it did not report sales from April 2020 to September 2021 because it was closed due to the pandemic. However, Staff provided evidence of Petitioner’s Facebook posts for periods from November 2020 to September 2021 (Staff’s Exhibit No. 12) with a summary of Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchase data for that period (Staff’s Exhibit No. 13) reflecting that it was open for business along. In addition, the pour test that was conducted during this time.

The assessments at issue were based upon Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages and a pour test conducted at the bar. The ALJ finds that Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that the audit was based on the best information available. Therefore, Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to demonstrate that the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e). Petitioner submitted very limited evidence for the joined hearing and, therefore, the ALJ finds Petitioner failed to establish error in the audit. The sales and use tax, MBST, and MBGRT assessments should be upheld in their entirety.

Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. Id. § 1.26(b)(1). Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

The Comptroller has repeatedly held that gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, sufficiently indicates intent to evade the tax and warrants the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015). The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b). The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019). Negligence, whether slight or great, is not the equivalent of fraud with intent to evade tax. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 45,514 (2006), 42,244 (2003), 38,886 (2002), 37,555 (1999), 35,527 (1997), 33,554 (1995); see also Webb v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 394 F.2d 366 (5th Cir. 1968).

In this case, Petitioner’s overall error rates for MBGRT and MBST are both in excess of 64%, and Petitioner did not provide a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting. Therefore, Staff’s evidence is sufficient to support the application of the 50% penalty for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011). The same principle applies to a limited liability company. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 112,305, 112,307, and 112,308 (2016). The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a). To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. Id. § 3.15(b). The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. Id. § 3.15(c).

************** is the managing member of Petitioner and prepared and filed the MBGRT and MBST returns at issue. There is no evidence that the fraudulent tax returns were due to an independent course of conduct taken by either ************** or any of Petitioner’s employees that did not further any purpose of Petitioner, and Petitioner has not produced any evidence to demonstrate that the acts or omissions of its officers, managers, and employees should not be imputed to Petitioner. The 50% penalty should be upheld for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. During the period at issue, ************** (Petitioner) held a mixed beverage permit and a sales and use tax permit, and operated a bar as COMPANY, in CITY, Texas.

2. ************** is the managing member of Petitioner and prepared and filed the mixed beverage sales tax (MBST) and mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT) returns for Petitioner.

3. In August 2021, the Tax Division (Staff) or the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated an MBGRT, MBST, and sales and use tax audit of Petitioner for the period January 1, 2018, through September 30, 2021.

4. At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit.

5. The auditor conducted the audit by performing a depletion analysis based on the average serving size for distilled spirits and beer, (calculated through a pour test performed at the bar) and vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverage inventory.

6. Petitioner did not provide any records in response to the auditor’s request but subsequently provided sales reports and complimentary drinks reports for January 1, 2019, through March 15, 2022.

7. The auditor conducted a pour test on August 26, 2021. During the pour observation, the auditor tested five drinks, which resulted in an average pour of 1.41 ounces for distilled spirits and 14.88 ounces for beer. Wine sales were deemed immaterial.

8. Using the serving sizes and Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and beer available for sale during the audit period.

9. The auditor used prices obtained from the pour test observation to determine the average selling price (ASP) and multiplied the ASP by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer.

10. Petitioner did not provide documentation showing complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, theft, breakage, or other potential allowances.

11. The differences between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for each beverage category.

12. The auditor applied the respective underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from sales of distilled spirits and beer for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

13. On March 14, 2022, Staff issued Texas Notifications of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing liabilities for MBGRT and MBST. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for sales and use tax. All assessments included tax, a 10% penalty, and accrued interest. The MBGRT and MBST assessments also included a 50% additional penalty.

14. The overall error rate in reporting tax was 65.41% for MBST and 64.66% for MBGRT.

15. Petitioner had 37 late returns during the audit period for MBGRT and 36 late returns for MBST.

16. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessments.

17. Petitioner did not provide any records and did not raise any specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment.

18. Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

19. On June 15, 2023, Staff issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. The notices contained a statement of the nature of the hearings; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearings were to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaints or petitions filed with the state agency.

20. On June 16, 2023, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) issued an order which combined the cases for purposes of issuing a single Proposal for Decision.

21. Petitioner subsequently filed an agreed motion to convert to an in-person hearing, which was granted.

22. The hearing convened on November 29, 2023.

23. The contested case record closed on December1, 2023, after the parties filed the evidence that was admitted at the hearing.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over these matters. Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to these hearings, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearings. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. “Taxable items” include tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010. The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

5. A 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001.

6. An 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

7. A mixed beverage permittee is a person, agent, or the officer, director, manager, or managing general partner of an entity that is the holder of a mixed beverage permit, a mixed beverage late hours permit, a mixed beverage permit holding a food and beverage certificate, a daily temporary mixed beverage permit, a private club registration permit, a private club exemption certificate permit, a private club late hours permit, a daily temporary private club permit, a private club registration permit holding a food and beverage certificate, a caterer’s permit, or a rectifier’s and distiller’s permit issued by the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001(a)(8).

8. As a mixed beverage permittee, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4).

9. In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the MBGRT and MBST liability based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

10. The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

11. Mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 115,139 and 115,140 (2019); Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017).

12. The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011).

13. Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation. See Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017) at 24.

14. Mixed beverage audits performed in accordance with proper auditing practices and procedures, based upon the best information available, are presumed to be correct. See Comptroller’s Decision No. 41,997 (2004).

15. Staff established, prima facie, that the assessments were based on the best information available.

16. Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to substantiate claims the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e).

17. Petitioner failed to establish error in the assessments.

18. A 50% penalty is authorized when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Tex. Tax Code § 111.061(b).

19. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(b)(1).

20. Clear and convincing evidence demonstrates the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

21. Gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, is sufficiently indicative of intent to evade the tax to warrant the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015).

22. Gross error means that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b).

23. The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019).

24. Petitioner did not provide a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting of MBGRT and MBST.

25. Staff’s evidence is sufficient to demonstrate, clearly and convincingly, that the 50% penalty applied to the MBGRT and MBST assessments is authorized by statute.

26. In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011).

27. The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a).

28. To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(b).

29. The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(c).

30. Petitioner did not produce evidence to demonstrate that the acts or omissions of its officers, managers, and employees should not be imputed to Petitioner.

31. The 50% penalty should be upheld for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

Proposal for Decision

The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) audited ************** (Petitioner) for compliance with mixed beverage tax laws and sales tax laws and made three assessments: one for mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT), one for mixed beverage sales tax (MBST), and one for sales and use tax. Each assessment included tax, 10% late penalty, and accrued interest. The MBST and MBGRT assessments also included a 50% fraud penalty. Petitioner requested redetermination for each hearing. Petitioner raised no specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment but disagreed with the audit methodology and contended general audit error for the MBST and MBGRT assessments. In this Proposal for Decision (PFD), the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) finds that the assessments, including the 50% fraud penalties, should be upheld.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on June 15, 2023, issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. On June 16, 2023, ALJ Kathy Pickup issued an order setting the written submission hearing and combining the cases for purposes of issuing a single PFD. Petitioner subsequently filed an agreed motion to convert to an in-person hearing, which was granted. Janice Cahalane represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by its managing member, **************. The hearing convened on November 29, 2023. The record closed on December 1, 2023, after the parties filed the evidence that was admitted at the hearing.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction in this proceeding. Therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner submitted sales reports and complimentary drink reports for January 1, 2019, through March 15, 2022.

Staff presented the testimony of the auditor, INDIVIDUAL and submitted the following exhibits for each hearing:

1. Hearing Request Receipt Letters;

2. Texas Notifications of Audit Results;

3. Penalty and Interest Waiver Worksheets;

4. Audit Package (MBGRT);

5. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (MBGRT);

6. Audit Package (MBST);

7. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (MBST);

8. Audit Package (Sales and Use Tax);

9. Audit Documentation Report / Audit Plan (Sales and Use Tax);

10. Audit Referral Report for Additional Penalty (Mixed Beverage Taxes);

11. Posts from Petitioner’s Facebook Page;

12. Posts from Petitioner’s Facebook Page for Periods from November 2020 to September 2021; and

13. Vendor-Reported Purchase Data Summay for the Tax Period.

The parties’ exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. AGREED ADJUSTMENTS

Staff did not agree to amend any of the assessments.

C. MATERIAL FACTS

During the period at issue, Petitioner held a mixed beverage permit and a sales and use tax permit, and operated a sports bar, COMPANY, in CITY, Texas. The bar also sold food items.

In August 2021, Staff initiated a MBGRT, MBST, and sales tax audit of Petitioner for the period January 1, 2018, through September 30, 2021. At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit. Petitioner did not provide any records.

A depletion analysis was performed based on the average serving size for distilled spirits and beer and vendor-reported purchases. The auditor conducted a pour test on August 26, 2021. During the pour observation, the auditor tested five drinks, which resulted in an average pour of 1.41 ounces for distilled spirits and 14.88 ounces for beer.[4] Using the serving sizes and Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and beer available for sale during the audit period. Due to the lack of documentation provided by Petitioner, the auditor used prices obtained from the pour test observation to determine the average selling price, then multiplied those prices by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer. Petitioner did not provide the auditor with documentation of complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, theft, breakage, or other potential allowances.

The differences between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for each beverage category. The auditor applied the respective underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from sales of distilled spirits and beer for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

On March 14, 2022, Staff issued Texas Notifications of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing liabilities for MBGRT and MBST. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for sales and use tax. All assessments included tax, a 10% penalty, and accrued interest. The MBGRT and MBST assessments also included a 50% additional penalty. The overall error rate in reporting tax was 65.41% for MBST and 64.66% for MBGRT. Petitioner had 37 late returns during the audit period for MBGRT and 36 late returns for MBST.

Petitioner requested redetermination, disagreeing with the audit methodology used and contending general audit error for the MBST and MBGRT assessments. Petitioner did not provide any records and did not raise any specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment. Staff contends no adjustments are warranted and referred the matters to SOAH.

D. ALJ’S ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. “Taxable items” include tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010. The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

In addition to the sales tax due on taxable items, a 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001. In addition, an 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

As a mixed beverage permit holder, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4). In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the gross receipts tax and sales tax liability based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. Id. §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. Id. Thus, mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See id.; Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017). The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011). Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation.[5] Mixed beverage audits performed in accordance with proper auditing practices and procedures, based upon the best information available, are presumed to be correct. Comptroller’s Decision No. 41,997 (2004).

Petitioner states it did not report sales from April 2020 to September 2021 because it was closed due to the pandemic. However, Staff provided evidence of Petitioner’s Facebook posts for periods from November 2020 to September 2021 (Staff’s Exhibit No. 12) with a summary of Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchase data for that period (Staff’s Exhibit No. 13) reflecting that it was open for business along. In addition, the pour test that was conducted during this time.

The assessments at issue were based upon Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages and a pour test conducted at the bar. The ALJ finds that Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that the audit was based on the best information available. Therefore, Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to demonstrate that the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e). Petitioner submitted very limited evidence for the joined hearing and, therefore, the ALJ finds Petitioner failed to establish error in the audit. The sales and use tax, MBST, and MBGRT assessments should be upheld in their entirety.

Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. Id. § 1.26(b)(1). Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

The Comptroller has repeatedly held that gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, sufficiently indicates intent to evade the tax and warrants the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015). The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b). The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019). Negligence, whether slight or great, is not the equivalent of fraud with intent to evade tax. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 45,514 (2006), 42,244 (2003), 38,886 (2002), 37,555 (1999), 35,527 (1997), 33,554 (1995); see also Webb v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 394 F.2d 366 (5th Cir. 1968).

In this case, Petitioner’s overall error rates for MBGRT and MBST are both in excess of 64%, and Petitioner did not provide a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting. Therefore, Staff’s evidence is sufficient to support the application of the 50% penalty for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011). The same principle applies to a limited liability company. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 112,305, 112,307, and 112,308 (2016). The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a). To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. Id. § 3.15(b). The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. Id. § 3.15(c).

************** is the managing member of Petitioner and prepared and filed the MBGRT and MBST returns at issue. There is no evidence that the fraudulent tax returns were due to an independent course of conduct taken by either ************** or any of Petitioner’s employees that did not further any purpose of Petitioner, and Petitioner has not produced any evidence to demonstrate that the acts or omissions of its officers, managers, and employees should not be imputed to Petitioner. The 50% penalty should be upheld for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. During the period at issue, ************** (Petitioner) held a mixed beverage permit and a sales and use tax permit, and operated a bar as COMPANY, in CITY, Texas.

2. ************** is the managing member of Petitioner and prepared and filed the mixed beverage sales tax (MBST) and mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT) returns for Petitioner.

3. In August 2021, the Tax Division (Staff) or the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated an MBGRT, MBST, and sales and use tax audit of Petitioner for the period January 1, 2018, through September 30, 2021.

4. At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit.

5. The auditor conducted the audit by performing a depletion analysis based on the average serving size for distilled spirits and beer, (calculated through a pour test performed at the bar) and vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverage inventory.

6. Petitioner did not provide any records in response to the auditor’s request but subsequently provided sales reports and complimentary drinks reports for January 1, 2019, through March 15, 2022.

7. The auditor conducted a pour test on August 26, 2021. During the pour observation, the auditor tested five drinks, which resulted in an average pour of 1.41 ounces for distilled spirits and 14.88 ounces for beer. Wine sales were deemed immaterial.

8. Using the serving sizes and Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and beer available for sale during the audit period.

9. The auditor used prices obtained from the pour test observation to determine the average selling price (ASP) and multiplied the ASP by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer.

10. Petitioner did not provide documentation showing complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, theft, breakage, or other potential allowances.

11. The differences between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for each beverage category.

12. The auditor applied the respective underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from sales of distilled spirits and beer for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

16. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessments.

17. Petitioner did not provide any records and did not raise any specific contentions in relation to the sales and use tax assessment.

18. Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

19. On June 15, 2023, Staff issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. The notices contained a statement of the nature of the hearings; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearings were to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaints or petitions filed with the state agency.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to these hearings, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearings. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

5. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

7. A mixed beverage permittee is a person, agent, or the officer, director, manager, or managing general partner of an entity that is the holder of a mixed beverage permit, a mixed beverage late hours permit, a mixed beverage permit holding a food and beverage certificate, a daily temporary mixed beverage permit, a private club registration permit, a private club exemption certificate permit, a private club late hours permit, a daily temporary private club permit, a private club registration permit holding a food and beverage certificate, a caterer’s permit, or a rectifier’s and distiller’s permit issued by the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001(a)(8).

Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

Proposal for Decision

The The Criminal Investigation Division (CID) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) determined that **************, dba **************, (Petitioner) violated statutory regulation by failing to display a proper tobacco warning sign. On July 6, 2023, the CID issued a Notice of Violation No. ************** for Cigarette/Tobacco Retailer Permit No. ************** (Tobacco Permit), held by Petitioner, imposing a $1,000 fine authorized under the Texas Health and Safety Code. [ENDNOTE 2] Petitioner requested a hearing to dispute the imposition of the fine. In this Proposal for Decision, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) recommends the fine proposed by the Tax Division (Staff) of the Comptroller be imposed.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred this case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on September 29, 2023, issued its Notice of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. On October 4, 2023, ALJ Kathy Pickup issued an Order Setting Written Submission Requirements. Teresa Gutierrez represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by **************. The contested case record closed on December 11, 2023.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction; therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner did not submit evidence for the hearing. Staff offered the following exhibits:

Notice of Violation;

Texas Comptroller Form 69-401, Cigarette Inspection Report;

Texas Comptroller Criminal Investigative Report, Case No. **************; and

Photographs of Petitioner’s Premises.

Staff’s exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. MATERIAL FACTS AND ISSUES PRESENTED

Petitioner operates a convenience store at ADDRESS, CITY, Texas. Petitioner is a tobacco retailer and sells cigarettes and other tobacco products under its tobacco permit, issued by the Comptroller. On June 22, 2023, Investigator Daniel Doss, a State Police Investigator commissioned by the Comptroller’s CID, conducted a tobacco inspection in accordance with Texas Tax Code §§ 154.304 and 155.210 and Texas Health and Safety Code §§ 161.088 and 147.0051(b).

Officer Doss visited Petitioner’s business and conducted surveillance and determined the business was open and operational. Officer Doss entered the premises and conducted a tobacco inspection of the business. He did not observe a warning “No one under 21 permitted” sign printed on the front door, nor did he observe the mandatory Tobacco/Cigarette Warning sign posted in a manner that was in view of the public and clerks from the point of sale for tobacco products.

On July 6, 2023, CID issued a formal Notice of Violation (Notice) ************** regarding Permit No. **************, held by Petitioner, citing failure to display proper warning sign in violation of Chapter 161 of the Health and Safety Code. The Notice stated the Comptroller intended to impose a fine of up to $1,000 on Petitioner for the violation and provided Petitioner the opportunity to request a hearing on the matter.

On July 13, 2023, Petitioner returned the respective form, indicating it wanted a hearing. On August 17, 2023, Staff referred the matter to SOAH and issued its Notice of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner on September 29, 2023. Staff maintains that the proposed fine for the violations should be upheld. Petitioner did not submit argument or evidence for the written submission hearing.

C. ALJ ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

Staff is alleging statutory violations that warrant imposition of a penalty or other disciplinary action and must establish the violations by a preponderance of the evidence. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1204(g). Texas issues permits to several types of tobacco dealers. A tobacco permit holder is defined as a bonded agent, distributor, wholesaler, manufacturer, importer, export warehouse, or retailer who obtains a permit under Texas Tax Code § 154.101. See Tex. Tax Code § 154.001(14). A tobacco retailer is defined as a person who engages in the business of selling cigarettes to consumers and includes the owner of a cigarette vending machine. See id. § 154.001(17). In this case, there is no dispute regarding the fact that Petitioner was a tobacco retailer and held a tobacco permit at the time of the violations at issue.

If the Comptroller finds, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing as provided by Texas Government Code Chapter 2001, that a permit holder has violated Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 161 at a place of business for which a permit is issued, the Comptroller may suspend the permit for that place of business and administratively assess a fine. See id. § 161.0901(b). For the first violation during the 24-month period preceding the violation at that place of business, the Comptroller may require the permit holder to pay a fine in an amount not to exceed $1,000. See id. § 161.0901(b)(1). The statutory scheme imposes strict liability, so that if the agent or employee of the retailer is found to have committed an offense under Chapter 161, the retailer is liable for sanctions noticed under § 161.0901.

Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.084(a) requires that each person who sells cigarettes, ecigarettes, or tobacco products at retail or by vending machine post a sign in a conspicuous location and close to the place where these products may be purchased. The sign must include the statement detailed in Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.084(b). In his Investigation Report, Officer Doss stated that he did not observe the proper warning signs posted in view of the public and employees from the point of sale for tobacco products. Petitioner failed to present evidence to the contrary, therefore, the ALJ recommends that the fine for the violation be upheld.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

**************, dba **************, (Petitioner) operates a convenience store at ADDRESS, CITY Texas.

Petitioner is a tobacco retailer and sells cigarettes and other tobacco products under its tobacco permit, issued by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller).

There is no dispute regarding the fact that Petitioner was a tobacco retailer and held a tobacco permit at the time of the violations at issue.

On June 22, 2023, Investigator Daniel Doss, a State Police Investigator commissioned by the Comptroller’s Criminal Investigation Division (CID), conducted a tobacco inspection in accordance with Texas Tax Code §§ 154.304 and 155.210 and Texas Health and Safety Code §§ 161.088 and 147.0051(b).

Officer Doss visited Petitioner’s business and conducted surveillance and determined the business was open and operational.

Officer Doss did not observe a warning “No one under 21 permitted” sign printed on the front door, nor did he observe the mandatory Tobacco/Cigarette Warning sign posted in a manner that was in view of the public and clerks from the point of sale for tobacco products.

On July 6, 2023, CID issued a formal Notice of Violation (Notice) ************** regarding Permit No. **************, held by Petitioner, citing failure to display proper warning sign in violation of Chapter 161 of the Health and Safety Code.

The Notice stated the Tax Division (Staff) of the Comptroller intended to impose a fine of up to $1,000 on Petitioner for the violation and provided Petitioner the opportunity to request a hearing on the matter.

On July 13, 2023, Petitioner returned the respective form, indicating it wanted a hearing.

On August 17, 2023, Staff referred the matter to SOAH and issued its Notice of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner on September 29, 2023. The notice contained a statement of the nature of the hearing; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing was to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaint or petition filed with the state agency.

On October 4, 2023, Administrative Law Judge Kathy Pickup issued an Order Setting Written Submission Requirements.

Petitioner did not submit evidence for the hearing.

The contested case record closed on December 11, 2023.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

The Comptroller has jurisdiction over these matters. See Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to the hearing, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

Staff provided a proper and timely notice of hearing. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901.

Staff is alleging statutory violations that warrant imposition of a penalty or other disciplinary action and must establish the violations by a preponderance of the evidence. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1204(g).

Texas issues permits to several types of tobacco dealers. A tobacco permit holder is defined as a bonded agent, distributor, wholesaler, manufacturer, importer, export warehouse, or retailer who obtains a permit under Texas Tax Code § 154.101. See Tex. Tax Code § 154.001(14).

A tobacco retailer is defined as a person who engages in the business of selling cigarettes to consumers and includes the owner of a cigarette vending machine. See Tex. Tax Code § 154.001(17).

If the Comptroller finds, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing as provided by Texas Government Code Chapter 2001, that a permit holder has violated Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 161 at a place of business for which a permit is issued, the Comptroller may suspend the permit for that place of business and administratively assess a fine. See Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901(b).

For the first violation during the 24-month period preceding the violation at that place of business, the Comptroller may require the permit holder to pay a fine in an amount not to exceed $1,000. See Tex. Health and Safety Code § 161.0901(b)(1).

Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.084(a) requires that each person who sells cigarettes, e-cigarettes, or tobacco products at retail or by vending machine post a sign in a conspicuous location and close to the place where these products may be purchased.

The sign must include the statement detailed in Texas Health and Safety Code § 161.084(b).

The record evidence supports the finding that the proper warning signs were not posted in view of the public and employees from the point of sale for tobacco products.

Petitioner failed to meet its evidentiary burden to establish that the fine should not be imposed.

The ALJ recommends that the fine for this violation be upheld.

Proposal for Decision

Petitioner did not provide evidence for the written submission hearing, and Staff recommended no adjustments to the assessments. In this Proposal for Decision (PFD), the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) finds that the assessments, 10% penalty, interest, and 50% additional penalty should be upheld for each assessment.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on September 21, 2023, issued Petitioner Notices of Hearing by Written Submission. On the same day, ALJ Trevor Moore issued Order Consolidating Cases and Setting Written Submission Hearing, setting the hearings and joining the cases for the purpose of issuing a single PFD. Petitioner was represented by **************. Janice Cahalane represented Staff. The contested case record closed November 30, 2023.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. Evidence

Petitioner did not submit exhibits for the hearings. Staff submitted the following exhibits for each hearing:

Ninety-Day Notification Letter;

Texas Notification of Audit Results;

Penalty and Interest Waiver Worksheet;

Audit Report (MBGRT);

Audit Plan (MBGRT);

Audit Report (MBST);

Audit Plan (MBST); and

Audit Report for Additional Penalty.

Staff’s exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. Staff Agreed Adjustments

Staff did not agree to adjust the assessments.

C. Material Facts

In the periods at issue, Petitioner operated a bar in CITY, Texas. In November 2021, Staff initiated an MBGRT and MBST audit of Petitioner for the period October 1, 2018, through August 31, 2021. The bar was closed at the outset of the audit.

During the audit period, Petitioner’s managers were involved in the day-to-day operations of the bar, employee INDIVIDUAL A prepared the daily deposits and the MBGRT and MBST returns at issue, and the managing member, INDIVIDUAL B, signed the returns.

At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit. In response, Petitioner provided point-of-sale (POS) records. Using the available records, the auditor completed a depletion analysis audit. The depletion analysis required establishing an average pour size for each type of alcoholic beverage served at the bars, average prices, and compiling Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages.

The bar was closed at the time of the audit, and therefore a pour test could not be conducted. The auditor relied on the results from Petitioner’s prior audit, which included an unannounced pour test that resulted in an average serving size of 1.25 ounces. However, due to the various serving sizes at the bar, the auditor applied a weighted average in the audit. The 1.25 ounce serving was used for 78% of the drinks and 2.00 ounces for 22% of the drinks, resulting in a 1.515 ounce serving size (inclusive of the 0.10 spill allowance). The audits used a serving size of one serving per bottle for packaged beer and bottled wine.

Using the average pour sizes and Petitioner’s vendor‑reported purchases of alcoholic beverages reflected in the Comptroller’s Retail Inventory Tracking System (reduced to eliminate secondary liquors), the auditor calculated the number of services of each type of beverage available for sale during the audit period.

Relying on Petitioner POS reports, the auditor calculated the average selling price for each type of drink by adding the total units of each beverage type sold and the respective total receipts to calculate an average sales price for distilled spirits and beer. The average selling price of distilled spirits mixed drinks was determined to be $7.1607; the average selling price of distilled spirits bottle service was determined to be $90.6013; the average selling price of bottle wine was determined to be $328.5714; and the average selling price of packaged beer was determined to be $4.3123. Petitioner did not provide documentation of inventory losses and therefore no verified allowances were made for complimentary drinks, theft, breakage, or spills.

The number of servings available for sale were multiplied by the respective average prices to calculate the gross receipts per each beverage class. The difference between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for each beverage category was divided by the respective reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for distilled spirits and beer. The auditor applied the underreporting error percentages to reported gross receipts from drink sales and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. Those receipts were added to the reconciliation adjustments, and the applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due. Petitioner’s overall error rates were 56% for MBGRT and 54.50% for MBST.

On June 17, 2022, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for the MBGRT. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBST. Both assessments include tax, penalty for late-filed periods, a 50% additional penalty, and accrued interest. Petitioner requested redetermination, contending the assessments are overstated due to errors in the average pour size for distilled spirits and average sales prices as applied in the audit and the failure to account for complimentary servings. Petitioner also contends the additional 50% penalty is not supported by the evidence, and the accrued interest should be waived. Petitioner did not submit evidence for the contested case hearings.

See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 45,514 (2006), 42,244 (2003), 38,886 (2002), 37,555 (1999), 35,527 (1997), 33,554 (1995); see also Webb v. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011). The same principle applies to a limited liability company. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 112,305, 112,307, and 112,308 (2016). To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. Id. § 3.15(b). Id. § 3.15(c).

The 50% penalty should be upheld for each assessment.

However, the Comptroller may waive interest upon its determination that the taxpayer exercised reasonable diligence to comply with Tax Code provisions. Tex. Tax Code §111.103 and 34 Tex. Admin. Code §3.5. When reviewing an interest waiver request, the following factors are considered: (1) undue delay caused by comptroller personnel; (2) reliance on advice provided by the comptroller’s office; and (3) natural disasters. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §3.5(e). Petitioner did not identify the applicability of any of the cited factors and therefore did not demonstrate that interest waiver is appropriate. The contention should be denied.

Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessment, contending the audit was based on incorrect hours of operation and incorrectly assumed perfect sales conditions. I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred this case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on August 28, 2023, issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. On September 15, 2023, ALJ Kimberly LaFlair issued an order setting the written submission hearing. Preston Tom represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by **************. II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner did not submit exhibits in the written submission hearing.

Staff submitted the pleadings exchanged between the parties prior to referring the matter to SOAH and offered the following exhibits:

1. Hearing Request Receipt;

2. Texas Notification of Audit Results;

3. Penalty and Interest Waiver Worksheet;

4. Audit Report; and

5. Audit Plan.

6. Staff’s exhibits are admitted without objection.

B. AGREED ADJUSTMENTS

C. MATERIAL FACTS AND ISSUES PRESENTED

Petitioner operated two food trucks that sold Honduran food. Outlet 1 is located at ADDRESS, CITY, Texas. Outlet 2 operated at two separate locations and closed in May 2021. Staff initiated a sales and use tax audit in September 2021 for the period of April 1, 2017, through December 31, 2020.

Petitioner did not charge sales tax separately but contends he included tax in the total sales price of his food. Petitioner did not keep any sales or purchase invoices, and he kept track of his sales in a handwritten notebook with the date and the price of the sale. Only cash was accepted for purchases and Petitioner did not maintain a bank account. Petitioner did not have a cash register and did not provide receipts for customer purchases.

Petitioner provided federal income tax returns for 2017, 2018, and 2019. The sales on the Schedule C attached to the returns matched Petitioner’s sales reported for 2017 and 2018. No sales were reported for the business in 2019.

Because Petitioner did not keep records, the auditor, along with her supervisor, conducted an observation and headcount for Outlet 1 as Outlet 2 closed on May 1, 2021. They observed approximately 27 different dishes on the menu, with the most popular item being the baleadas.[4] Prices were not included on the menu, but they ordered three baleadas and were charged $12. Only cash was accepted, and they did not receive a receipt for the order. Sales were observed for three hours, from 12:45 p.m. to 3:45 p.m.

The auditor totaled the observed sales transactions, calculated an hourly average, and then used that value to estimate taxable sales (i.e., multiplying the hourly value by the estimated food truck operational hours). Petitioner’s reported taxable sales were subtracted from the net estimated taxable sales and the remaining amounts were scheduled as additional taxable sales. The auditor performed a similar estimation for Outlet 2, but only for the periods of January 2019, February 2019, and April 2020 based on information provided by Petitioner that the food truck at that location was not in working order for many months.

During a conference with the auditor, Petitioner claimed that the hours listed on the Outlet 1 truck are not the actual hours the food truck operated. Petitioner also claimed the food truck did not open every day. The auditor decided to use eight hours per day and five days per week for the estimation. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the auditor reduced the open hours for the first and second quarter in 2020. The auditor decided that due to the minimal number of estimated sales for the second food truck, she would not assess Outlet 2. The additional taxable sales were updated based on the foregoing information.

The auditor again met with Petitioner, and he claimed that the baleadas only sold for $1.50 to $2.00 when he first opened the business, which was 50% of the current pricing. Petitioner also claimed that when the business first opened it was open for fewer hours. The auditor agreed to change the business days open from 5 days to 4 days for 2017 and 2018. D. ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Id. § 151.010. All sellers and all other persons storing, using, or consuming in this state a taxable item purchased from a retailer shall keep records in the form the Comptroller requires. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(a)(1). For example, a seller must keep records of all gross receipts, including documentation in the form of receipts from each sale occurring during each reporting period. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(1). In addition, a seller’s records must substantiate any claimed deductions or exclusions authorized by law. Id. § 151.025(a)(3); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b). If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on the best information available. Petitioner disagrees with the audit results and contends that the auditor did not correctly account for his business hours, incorrectly assumed perfect sales conditions for each day, and did not accurately account for the Covid-19 pandemic. Petitioner’s handwritten notes are not supported by any documentation or source records and are therefore not considered evidence.

The auditor also reduced the additional taxable sales during the first two quarters of 2020 to account for the pandemic, and she did not assess transactions related to Outlet 2. Staff contends Petitioner’s records were unreliable and incomplete and that the estimated audit is based on the best information available. The ALJ agrees, and Staff’s prima facie case to show the scheduled transactions were taxable is met. Petitioner’s evidence is insufficient to demonstrate, by a preponderance of evidence, that any items in dispute were scheduled erroneously. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e). Petitioner’s contentions should be denied, and the audit assessment should be upheld.

12. Petitioner claimed that the hours listed on the Outlet 1 truck are not the actual hours the food truck operated. Petitioner also claimed the food truck did not open every day.

13. The auditor decided to use eight hours per day and five days per week for the estimation.

14. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the auditor reduced the open hours for the first and second quarter in 2020.

15. The auditor decided that due to the minimal number of estimated sales for the second food truck, she would not assess Outlet 2.

16. The auditor agreed to change the business days open from 5 days to 4 days for 2017 and 2018. The food price for those years was also lowered by 50% and an updated assessment for additional taxable sales was provided to Petitioner.

17. On February 28, 2022, Staff issued an audit report and Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner. The assessment included tax, 10% late filing penalty, and accrued interest.

18. Petitioner timely requested redetermination.

19. Petitioner did not provide any additional information or evidence during redetermination or during the hearings process to support any adjustments to the assessment.

20. Staff did not agree to adjust the assessment and referred the matter to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

21. On August 28, 2023, Staff issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. Each notice contained a statement of the nature of the hearing; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing was to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaint or petition filed with the state agency.

22. On September 15, 2023, ALJ Kimberly LaFlair issued an order setting the written submission hearing.

23. The contested case record closed on November 20, 2023.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over this matter. See Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to the hearing in this matter, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearing. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051.

5. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010.

6. All sellers and all other persons storing, using, or consuming in this state a taxable item purchased from a retailer shall keep records in the form the Comptroller requires. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(a)(1).

7. A seller must keep records of all gross receipts, including documentation in the form of receipts from each sale occurring during each reporting period. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(1).

8. A seller’s records must substantiate any claimed deductions or exclusions authorized by law. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(3); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

9. If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on the best information available. Tex. Tax Code §§ 111.0042(d), .008(a).

10. A taxpayer cannot defeat an assessment based on the burden of proof by withholding or failing to provide documentation. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,386 (2014), 105,892 (2012).

11. Treating transactions that lack documentation as taxable is supported by statute. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 103,035 (2014), 39,765 (2003).

13. The ALJ finds Staff’s prima facie case to show the transactions were taxable is met.

14. The ALJ finds that Petitioner’s records were unreliable and incomplete and that the estimated audit is based on the best information available.

15. The ALJ finds that Petitioner’s evidence is insufficient to demonstrate, by a preponderance of evidence, that any items in dispute were scheduled erroneously. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

16. Petitioner’s contentions should be denied, and the audit assessment should be upheld.

5. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010.

6. All sellers and all other persons storing, using, or consuming in this state a taxable item purchased from a retailer shall keep records in the form the Comptroller requires. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(a)(1).

7. For example, a seller must keep records of all gross receipts, including documentation in the form of receipts from each sale occurring during each reporting period. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(1).

8. A seller’s records must substantiate any claimed deductions or exclusions authorized by law. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(3); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

9. If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on the best information available. Tex. Tax Code §§ 111.0042(d), .008(a).

10. A taxpayer cannot defeat an assessment based on the burden of proof by withholding or failing to provide documentation. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,386 (2014), 105,892 (2012).

11. Treating transactions that lack documentation as taxable is supported by statute. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 103,035 (2014), 39,765 (2003).

12. The Comptroller has routinely held that summary documents that are created by the taxpayer and submitted without underlying support are tantamount to bare assertions, i.e., they are not considered evidence. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 117,167-117,174 117,168, and 117,169(2023).

13. Petitioner’s records were unreliable and incomplete and, in the absence of reliable records, Petitioner’s federal income tax returns were the best information available.

14. Staff’s prima facie case to show the transactions were taxable is met.

15. Petitioner’s evidence is insufficient to demonstrate, by a preponderance of evidence, that any remaining items in dispute were scheduled erroneously. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

16. Petitioner’s contentions should be denied.

17. The audit assessment should be upheld, except as agreed by Staff.
