Proposal for Decision

The Business Activity Research Team (BART) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) examined ************** (Petitioner) business activities in Texas and determined that Petitioner was engaged in business in Texas and therefore had nexus with Texas for sales and use tax. BART requested that Petitioner complete the Texas Nexus Questionnaire and Texas Sales and Use Tax Permit and provide a sales and use tax worksheet detailing its taxable sales during the period under review. Petitioner failed to respond to BART’s requests and, therefore, BART estimated Petitioner’s sales and use tax liability. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessment, contending its services were performed in Arizona, not Texas, and therefore there is no nexus for Texas sales and use tax. The Comptroller’s Tax Division (Staff) again requested Petitioner provide documentation to support its contentions, but Petitioner declined to do so. In this Proposal for Decision, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) recommends affirming the estimated assessment.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on August 29, 2023, issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. On August 30, 2023, ALJ Trevor Moore issued the Order Setting Written Submission Requirements, setting the hearing and establishing the record closing date of October 30, 2023. Preston Tom represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by **************.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction; therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner did not submit evidence for the hearing. Staff submitted the pleadings exchanged by the parties while the hearing was in redetermination at the Comptroller’s office and submitted the following exhibits for the written submission hearing:

1. Notification Letter;

2. Texas Notification of Exam Results;

3. Business Activity Research Team Documents;

4. District Court Filings for INDIVIDUAL vs. PETITIONER, D-1-GN-13-000677 (2013); and

5. Website Screenshot for Petitioner.

B. AGREEMENTS

There are no agreements.

C. MATERIAL FACTS AND CONTENTIONS

Petitioner is headquartered in CITY, California. During the period at issue, it provided skip tracing, repossession, and recovery services. BART determined that Petitioner was performing debt collection services in Texas and requested Petitioner provide its Texas sales information for the period of November 1, 2013, through August 31, 2019. When Petitioner did not respond to the request for documentation, BART estimated the tax owed at the rate of $1,000 for each month of the exam period. On October 24, 2019, Staff issued Petitioner a Texas Notification of Exam Results assessing tax, penalty, and interest. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessment.

Petitioner does not dispute that it provided debt collection services during the exam period but argues it did not perform those services in Texas. Specifically, Petitioner contends that its services included locating vehicles or collateral possessed by individuals who have “skipped” on a contracted debt and, once the collateral was found, that information was “provided to its client, COMPANY A in CITY, Arizona.” As described by Petitioner, the cases were then “assigned to Petitioner by COMPANY A” and were then “worked” at Petitioner’s headquarters in California, and any collateral located in Texas “is then assigned to third-party agent that has a contract with COMPANY A.” Therefore, Petitioner reasons, it was not engaged in business in Texas and does not have nexus with Texas for purposes of sales and use tax. Rather, Petitioner argues, COMPANY A “pays the sales taxes for the services provided by the third-party recovery companies in Texas.” In response to Petitioner’s contentions, Staff requested documentation of Petitioner’s business activities as described by Petitioner, including its contracts with customers, but none were provided. Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the written submission hearing.

D. APPLICABLE LAW, ANALYSIS, AND CONCLUSION

Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Id. § 151.010. Where the contested case issue in dispute involves the taxability of a service, Staff must demonstrate, prima facie, that the service is taxable. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,530 (2015). If that burden is satisfied, Petitioner must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that tax was paid, accrued, or assessed on a service in error. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

A taxpayer cannot defeat an assessment based on the burden of proof by not providing the necessary documents. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 107,078 (2015). The party in possession of evidence peculiarly within its control has the burden of producing that evidence. See Watson v. Brazos Elec. Power Corp., Inc., 918 S.W.2d 639, 643 (Tex. App.—Waco 1996, writ denied) (failure to produce evidence within a party’s control raises the presumption that if produced it would operate against him, and every intendment will be in favor of the opposite party); Brewer v. Dowling, 862 S.W.2d 156, 159 (Tex. App.—Fort Worth 1993, writ denied); H. E. Butt Grocery Co. v. Bruner, 530 S. W. 2d 340, 343 (Tex. App.—Waco 1975, writ dism’d). This presumption arises whenever the party not in possession of the evidence has introduced evidence harmful to the party who had control of the evidence. See Brewer, 862 S.W.2d at 159. “Under such circumstances, the failure of the [party in control of the evidence] to rebut the harmful evidence with evidence within its control raises a presumption that the unpresented evidence would also be unfavorable to the nonproducing party.” Id.

1. Debt Collection Services

Debt collection services are included among the taxable services listed in Texas Tax Code § 151.0101(a)(8) and include activities “to collect or adjust a delinquent debt, to collect or adjust a claim, or to repossess property subject to a claim.” Id. § 151.0036(a). The applicable rule further defines a debt collection service as including “any activity performed in furtherance of the satisfaction or compromise of a debt or claim.” 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.354(a)(4).

As argued by Staff, Petitioner’s website states that it “provides location, repossession and asset recovery services to our clients in the United States,” and Petitioner did not dispute this description. In addition, when requested by BART and then again by Staff, Petitioner declined to provide any documentation regarding its services. The ALJ finds that Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that Petitioner was providing debt collection services during the exam period.

2. Texas Sales and Use Tax Nexus

A person is engaged in business in Texas if the person has nexus with the state as evidenced by the fact that it has any representative, agent, salesperson, canvasser, or solicitor who operates in this state under the authority of the seller to conduct business, including selling, delivering, or taking orders for taxable items, or conducts business in this state through employees, agents, or independent contractors. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.286(a)(42)(B), (G).[5] As relevant here, a person who employs independent contractors to perform debt collection services on their behalf is engaging in business in Texas. Comptroller’s Decision No. 114,229 (2019).

Each seller who is engaged in business in this state must apply to the Comptroller and obtain a sales and use tax permit for each place of business the seller operated in this state and a single permit for its out-of-state places of business. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.286(b)(1). In addition, the law requires all sellers permitted Texas taxpayers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b). If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on any available information. Tex. Tax Code § 111.008(a).

The evidence in the contested case record supports a conclusion that Petitioner used independent contractors in performing taxable debt collection services in Texas and was, therefore, engaged in business in Texas during the exam period. The ALJ finds the estimated audit was authorized by statute, the best information available was utilized, and the audit is presumed correct. Petitioner bears the burden of proof to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the audit results are incorrect. Comptroller’s Decision No. 116,436 (20221); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

Petitioner argued it did not have nexus for sales and use tax purposes because its services were all performed out of state and it was a third party, COMPANY A in Arizona, that performed debt collection services in Texas. Addressing Petitioner’s claim of a lack of nexus with Texas, Staff argues that Petitioner uses independent contractors to recover or repossess collateral in Texas. The ALJ finds that conclusion is supported by the website information submitted by Staff (Exhibit 5) as well as a contract with a customer, included with documents filed by Petitioner in a Texas court case (Exhibit 4). The ALJ concludes Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that Petitioner’s business activities in Texas established sales and use tax nexus in Texas. The burden shifts to Petitioner to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that it lacked the requisite nexus with Texas. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 106,632 and 108,826 (2014); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e)3.286(a)(4)(A), (E).

Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the written submission hearing and, therefore, the ALJ finds the evidence is insufficient to demonstrate that Petitioner was not engaged in business in Texas and did not have sales and use tax nexus with Texas. Petitioner’s contention should remain denied and the estimated assessment upheld.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. ************** (Petitioner) is headquartered in CITY, California.

2. During the period at issue, Petitioner provided skip tracing, repossession, and recovery services.

3. Petitioner’s website states that it “provides location, repossession and asset recovery services to our clients in the United States,” and Petitioner does not dispute this description.

4. In September 2019, the Business Activity Research Team (BART) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) determined Petitioner was doing business in Texas and requested Petitioner provide its Texas sales information for the period of November 1, 2013, through August 31, 2019.

5. Petitioner did not respond to the request for documentation of its sales.

6. BART estimated the tax owed at the rate of $1,000 for each month of the exam period.

7. On October 24, 2019, Staff issued Petitioner a Texas Notification of Exam Results assessing tax, penalty, and interest.

8. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessment.

9. The Tax Division (Staff) of the Comptroller referred the hearing to the State Office of Administrative Hearings and issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner.

10. The notice contained the date, time, and location of the hearing; a statement of the nature of the hearing; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing was to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaint or petition filed with the state agency.

11. On August 30, 2023, Administrative ALJ Trevor Moore issued the Order Setting Written Submission Requirements, setting the hearing and establishing the record closing date of October 30, 2023.

12. Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the written submission hearing.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over this matter. See Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to the hearings in this matter, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearing. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051.

5. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010.

6. Where the contested case issue in dispute involves the taxability of a service, Staff must demonstrate, prima facie, that the service is taxable. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,530 (2015).

7. If that burden is satisfied, Petitioner must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that that tax was assessed in error. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

8. A taxpayer cannot defeat an assessment based on the burden of proof by not providing the necessary documents. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 107,078 (2015).

9. The party in possession of evidence peculiarly within its control has the burden of producing that evidence. See Watson v. Brazos Elec. Power Corp., Inc., 918 S.W.2d 639, 643 (Tex. App.—Waco 1996, writ denied) (failure to produce evidence within a party’s control raises the presumption that if produced it would operate against him, and every intendment will be in favor of the opposite party); Brewer v. Dowling, 862 S.W.2d 156, 159 (Tex. App.—Fort Worth 1993, writ denied); H. E. Butt Grocery Co. v. Bruner, 530 S. W. 2d 340, 343 (Tex. App.—Waco 1975, writ dism’d).

10. This presumption arises whenever the party not in possession of the evidence has introduced evidence harmful to the party who had control of the evidence. See Brewer, 862 S.W.2d at 159.

11. Debt collection services are taxable and include activities “to collect or adjust a delinquent debt, to collect or adjust a claim, or to repossess property subject to a claim.” Tex. Tax Code § 151.0101(a)(8); .0036(a).

12. A taxable debt collection service includes “any activity performed in furtherance of the satisfaction or compromise of a debt or claim.” 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.354(a)(4).

13. A seller is engaged in business in Texas if the seller derives receipts from the sale, lease, or rental of tangible personal property that is located in Texas or owns or uses tangible personal property that is located in Texas; solicits orders for taxable items by mail or through other media including the internet or other media that may be developed in the future; or otherwise conducts business in Texas. See Tex. Tax Code § 151.107(a)(3), (5), (9); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.286(a)(4)(E), (G), (J).

14. A person is engaged in business in Texas if the person has nexus with the state as evidenced by the fact that it has any representative, agent, salesperson, canvasser, or solicitor who operates in this state under the authority of the seller to conduct business, including selling, delivering, or taking orders for taxable items, or conducts business in this state through employees, agents, or independent contractors. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.286(a)(42)(B), (G).

15. A person who employs independent contractors to perform debt collection services on their behalf is engaging in business in Texas. Comptroller’s Decision No. 114,229 (2019).

16. Each seller who is engaged in business in this state must apply to the Comptroller and obtain a sales and use tax permit for each place of business of the seller operated in this state and a single permit for its out-of-state places of business. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.286(b)(1).

17. The law requires sellers permitted Texas taxpayers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

18. If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on any available information. Tex. Tax Code § 111.008(a).

19. In this case, the ALJ concludes the estimated audit was authorized by statute, the best information available was utilized, and the audit is presumed correct. Petitioner bears the burden of proof to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the audit results are incorrect. Comptroller’s Decision No. 116,436 (20221); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

20. Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that Petitioner’s business activities in Texas established sales and use tax nexus in Texas.

21. The burden shifts to Petitioner to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that it lacked the requisite nexus with Texas. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 106,632 and 108,826 (2014).

22. The ALJ finds Petitioner’s evidence regarding its sales is insufficient to demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that it was not engaged in business in Texas and did not have sales and use tax nexus with Texas.

23. Petitioner’s contention should be denied.

24. The estimated assessment should be upheld.

Proposal for Decision

The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) audited the ************** (Petitioner) for compliance with mixed beverage tax laws and made assessments for mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT), mixed beverage sales tax (MBST), accrued interest, 10% late penalty, and 50% fraud penalty. Petitioner requested redetermination, asserting the audit is in error. Staff subsequently amended the assessments to remove purchases of secondary liquors. Staff now agrees to the suggested amendments to the average prices. In this Proposal for Decision (PFD), the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) finds that the proposed amended assessments, including the 50% fraud penalties, should be upheld, except as agreed by Staff.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on July 25, 2023, issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. On July 27, 2023, ALJ Trevor Moore issued an order setting the written submission hearing and combining the cases for purposes of issuing a single PFD. Janice Cahalane represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by **************. The contested case record closed September 18, 2023.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction in this proceeding. Therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner submitted summary spreadsheets reflecting its calculations of its prices, attached to its pleadings filed with Staff, but did not otherwise offer exhibits once the hearings were set.

Staff submitted the following exhibits for each hearing:

1. Ninety-Day Letter;

2. Texas Notification of Audit Results;

3. Penalty and Interest Waiver Worksheet;

4. Audit Report (MBST);

5. Audit Plan (MBST);

6. Audit Report (MBGRT);

7. Audit Plan (MBGRT);

8. Audit Referral Report for Additional Penalty;

9. Amended Audit (MBST);

10. Amended Audit Plan (MBST);

11. Amended Audit (MBGRT);

12. Amended Audit Plan (MBGRT);

13. Proposed Adjustments (MBST); and

14. Proposed Adjustments (MBGRT).

The parties’ exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. AGREED ADJUSTMENTS

Staff agrees the amended tax assessments should be further adjusted as set out in Staff’s Exhibits 13 and 14.

C. MATERIAL FACTS

During the period at issue, Petitioner held a mixed beverage permit and operated a bar, COMPANY, in CITY, Texas. INDIVIDUAL is the president of Petitioner. INDIVIDUAL was involved in the day-to-day business of the bar during the period at issue and prepared and filed the MBST and MBGRT returns for Petitioner.

In September 2018, Staff initiated an MBGRT and MBST audit of Petitioner for the period April 1, 2015, through July 31, 2018. At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit. In response, Petitioner provided sales summaries for several months of the audit period.

The auditor conducted the audit by performing a depletion analysis based on the average serving size for distilled spirits and wine (calculated through a pour test performed at the bar), the available sales records (to determine average sales prices), and vendor-reported purchases. Using the serving sizes and Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and wine available for sale during the audit period.[4] The auditor then multiplied the average selling price by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits, wine, and beer. Petitioner did not provide documentation showing complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, theft, breakage, or other potential allowances.

The differences between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for each beverage category. The auditor applied the respective underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from sales of distilled spirits and beer for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

On May 3, 2019, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBGRT. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBST. Both assessments include tax, a 10% penalty, a 50% additional penalty, and accrued interest. The overall error rate in reporting tax was 56.99% for MBST and 56.92% for MBGRT. Petitioner had 23 late returns during the audit period for each tax type.

Petitioner requested redetermination, contending the audit was in error and citing several general contentions. Staff subsequently amended the assessments to remove purchases of secondary liquors. In March 2021, Petitioner entered its last correspondence in the case, proposing amendments to the average selling prices for liquor, beer, and wine, and submitting its own calculations. Staff applied the average prices as proposed by Petitioner in the agreed adjustments to the assessments set out in Staff’s Exhibits 13 and 14. Applying the agreed adjustments, the error rate for MBST is reduced to 53.33% and the error rate for MBGRT is reduced to 53.25%. Petitioner did not raise contentions with the audit and did not submit evidence for the written submission hearing.

D. ALJ’S ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

A 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001. In addition, an 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

As a mixed beverage permit holder, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4). In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the gross receipts tax and sales tax liability based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. Id. §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. Id. Thus, mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See id.; Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017). The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011). Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation. See Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017) at p. 24. Mixed beverage audits performed in accordance with proper auditing practices and procedures, based upon the best information available, are presumed to be correct. Comptroller’s Decision No. 41,997 (2004).

The assessments at issue were based upon Petitioner’s sales records, its vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, and a pour test conducted at the bar. The ALJ finds that Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that the audit was based on the best information available. Therefore, Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to demonstrate that the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e). Petitioner did not submit evidence for the joined hearing and, therefore, the ALJ finds Petitioner failed to establish error in the audit. The MBST and MBGRT assessments should be upheld, except as agreed by Staff.

Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. Id. § 1.26(b)(1). Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

The Comptroller has repeatedly held that gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, sufficiently indicates intent to evade the tax and warrants the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015). The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b). The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019). Negligence, whether slight or great, is not the equivalent of fraud with intent to evade tax. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 45,514 (2006), 42,244 (2003), 38,886 (2002), 37,555 (1999), 35,527 (1997), 33,554 (1995); see also Webb v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 394 F.2d 366 (5th Cir. 1968).

In this case, Petitioner’s overall error rates, accounting for Staff’s agreed audit adjustments, are both in excess of 53%, and Petitioner did not provide a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting. Therefore, Staff’s evidence is sufficient to support the application of the 50% penalty for the MBGRT and MBST assessments.

In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011). The same principle applies to a limited liability company. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 112,305, 112,307, and 112,308 (2016). The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a). To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. Id. § 3.15(b). The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. Id. § 3.15(c).

INDIVIDUAL is the president of Petitioner, managed Petitioner’s bar, and prepared and filed the MBGRT and MBST returns at issue. There is no evidence that the fraudulent tax returns were due to an independent course of conduct taken by either INDIVIDUAL or any of Petitioner’s employees that did not further any purpose of Petitioner, and Petitioner has not produced any evidence to demonstrate that the acts or omissions of its officers, managers, and employees should not be imputed to Petitioner. The 50% penalty should be upheld for the proposed amended MBGRT and MBST assessments.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. During the period at issue, the ************** (Petitioner) held a mixed beverage permit and operated a bar, COMPANY (the bar), in CITY, Texas.

2. INDIVIDUAL is the president of Petitioner.

3. INDIVIDUAL was involved in the day-to-day business of the bar during the period at issue and prepared and filed the mixed beverage sales tax (MBST) and mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT) returns for Petitioner.

4. In September 2018, the Tax Division (Staff) or the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated an MBGRT and MBST audit of Petitioner for the period April 1, 2015, through July 31, 2018.

5. At the outset of the audit field work, the auditor sent correspondence to Petitioner asking that it provide responses to the management questionnaire and records for the audit.

6. Petitioner provided the auditor with sales summaries for several months of the audit period.

7. The auditor conducted the audit by performing a depletion analysis based on the average serving size for distilled spirits and wine (calculated through a pour test performed at the bar) and packaged beer, the available sales records (to determine average sales prices), and vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverage inventory.

8. Using the serving sizes and Petitioner’s vendor-reported purchases of alcoholic beverages, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits, wine, and beer available for sale during the audit period. The auditor then multiplied the average selling price by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer.

9. Petitioner did not provide documentation showing complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, theft, breakage, or other potential allowances.

10. The differences between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts, resulting in a reporting error percentage for each beverage category.

11. The auditor applied the respective underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from sales of distilled spirits and beer for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The applicable tax rates were applied to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

12. On May 3, 2019, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBGRT. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBST. Both assessments include tax, a 10% penalty, a 50% additional penalty, and accrued interest.

13. The overall error rate in reporting tax was 56.99% for MBST and 56.92% for MBGRT.

14. Petitioner had 23 late returns during the audit period for each tax type.

15. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessments.

16. Staff amended the assessments to remove purchases of secondary liquors.

17. Petitioner’s proposed average prices are agreed by Staff. The resulting proposed amendments to the assessments are reflected in Staff’s Exhibits 13 and 14, proposing amendments to the average selling prices for liquor, beer, and wine, and submitting its own calculations.

18. Applying the agreed adjustments, the error rate for MBST is reduced to 53.33% and the error rate for MBGRT is reduced to 53.25%.

19. Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

20. On July 25, 2023, Staff issued Notices of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. The notices contained a statement of the nature of the hearings; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearings were to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaints or petitions filed with the state agency.

21. On July 27, 2023, the Administrative Law Judge issued an order which combined the cases for purposes of issuing a single Proposal for Decision.

22. The contested case record closed on September 18, 2023.

23. Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the joined hearing.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over these matters. See Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to these hearings, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearings. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. A 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001.

5. An 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

6. A mixed beverage permittee is a person, agent, or the officer, director, manager, or managing general partner of an entity that is the holder of a mixed beverage permit, a mixed beverage late hours permit, a mixed beverage permit holding a food and beverage certificate, a daily temporary mixed beverage permit, a private club registration permit, a private club exemption certificate permit, a private club late hours permit, a daily temporary private club permit, a private club registration permit holding a food and beverage certificate, a caterer’s permit, or a rectifier’s and distiller’s permit issued by the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001(a)(8).

8. In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the MBGRT and MBST liability based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

9. The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

10. Mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 115,139 and 115,140 (2019); Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017).

11. The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011).

12. Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation. See Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017) at 24.

13. Mixed beverage audits performed in accordance with proper auditing practices and procedures, based upon the best information available, are presumed to be correct. See Comptroller’s Decision No. 41,997 (2004).

14. Staff established, prima facie, that the assessments were based on the best information available.

15. Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to substantiate claims the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e).

16. Petitioner failed to establish error in the assessments, except as agreed by Staff.

17. A 50% penalty is authorized when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Tex. Tax Code § 111.061(b).

18. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(b)(1).

19. Clear and convincing evidence demonstrates the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

20. Gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, is sufficiently indicative of intent to evade the tax to warrant the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015).

21. Gross error means that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b).

22. The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019).

23. Petitioner did not provide a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting of MBGRT and MBST.

24. Staff’s evidence is sufficient to demonstrate, clearly and convincingly, that the 50% penalty applied to each assessment is authorized by statute.

25. In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011).

26. The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of:

1. any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and

2. any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a).

27. To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(b).

28. The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(c).

29. Petitioner did not produce evidence to demonstrate that the acts or omissions of its officers, managers, and employees should not be imputed to Petitioner.

31. The amended assessments should be upheld, except as agreed by Staff.

Proposal for Decision

The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) audited ************** (Petitioner) for sales and use tax compliance and issued an assessment for tax, penalty, additional penalty, and accrued interest. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessment and provided additional documentation for consideration. Staff subsequently adjusted the audit. Petitioner maintains the assessment is in error, though it did not submit evidence for the hearing. In this Proposal for Decision, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) recommends the assessment be upheld, except as for agreed by Staff.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and on June 20, 2023, issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. On June 22, 2023, ALJ Trevor Moore issued an Order Setting Written Submission Hearing setting the hearing and establishing filing deadlines. The contested case record closed on August 28, 2023. Nickie Yee represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by **************.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction; therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. Evidence

Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the hearing. Staff submitted the pleadings exchanged by the parties while the case was in redetermination at the Comptroller and filed the following exhibits for the written submission hearing:

1. Texas Notification of Audit Results;

2. Penalty & Interest Waiver Worksheet;

3. Audit Report;

4. Audit Plan;

5. Audit Referral Report for Additional Penalty; and

6. Adjusted Exams.

The exhibits were admitted without objection.

B. Agreed Adjustments

Staff agreed to the adjustments to the audit as set out in Staff’s Exhibit 6.

C. Facts Demonstrated by the Evidence

During the period at issue, Petitioner operated two “drive-through” food and beverages stores, one in CITY, Texas (Outlet 1) and one in CITY, Texas (Outlet 2). Petitioner’s sole managing member is INDIVIDUAL A, and the manager of the CITY outlet is named INDIVIDUAL B. The stores sold beer, but did not sell distilled spirits and, therefore, did not hold a mixed beverage permit or remit mixed beverage gross receipts tax.

In 2019, Staff initiated an audit to verify Petitioner’s compliance with Texas sales and use tax laws in the period January 1, 2016, through December 31, 2019. Petitioner did not return the audit questionnaire, did not respond to the auditor’s attempts at communication via phone and email, and did not provide business records for the audit. Because Petitioner failed to provide its business records, the audit was estimated using Petitioner’s purchase data and the average sales prices at Petitioner’s outlets.[4]

Without any business records, the auditor made observations at each Outlet and recorded the products sold, the amount of the sales, and cash or credit sales during several hours at each outlet. By documenting the food and alcohol sales, the auditor calculated a “product mix percentage” representing the ratio of beer sales to other sales. The product mix percentage for beer was 21.8% for Outlet 1 and 13.72% for Outlet 2. The auditor obtained a beer price list during the observation and that list, along with the documentation of inventory purchases of beer, allowed the audit to calculate a mark-up percentage of 44% for beer during the audit period.

For each outlet, the total estimated beer sales were calculated by multiplying Petitioner’s wholesale beer purchases by the average markup percentage. With estimated beer sales established, taxable sales for the audit period were calculated by dividing the total estimated beer sales by the product mix percentage for each respective outlet. Petitioner’s reported taxable sales were then subtracted from the estimated taxable sales to arrive at the estimated additional taxable sales. The additional tax due was calculated by multiplying the applicable state and local tax rates to the estimated additional taxable sales for each outlet.

On May 21, 2020, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing tax, 10% penalty, 50% additional penalty, and interest accrued to the account. Petitioner requested a redetermination of the assessment, raising several contentions and providing additional documentation. Staff agreed to adjust the assessment, and those adjustments are set out in Staff’s Exhibit 6. The adjusted error rate is 78.44%. Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the written submission hearing.

D. ALJ Analysis and Recommendation

Sales tax is due on each sale of a taxable item in this state, and use tax is due on the storage, use or other consumption of a taxable item in Texas. Tex. Tax Code §§ 151.051, .101. The term taxable item includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Id. § 151.010. Here, there is no dispute that Petitioner was a retailer of tangible personal property during the audit period.

The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b). If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on any available information, including records of suppliers. Tex. Tax Code §§ 111.0042(d), .008(a). The ALJ concludes Staff’s evidence is sufficient to establish, prima facie, that the estimated audit was authorized by statute and that the best information available was utilized. Therefore, it is Petitioner’s burden to show audit error by a preponderance of the evidence. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e). Petitioner failed to provide evidence or argument for the hearing, and therefore failed to demonstrate audit error. The ALJ recommends affirming the audit, except as agreed by Staff.

Late penalties are automatically imposed on delinquent taxes. Tex. Tax Code § 111.061. The Comptroller has the discretionary authority to waive late penalties if a taxpayer has exercised reasonable diligence to comply with tax laws. Id. § 111.103. A taxpayer must establish reasonable diligence by a preponderance of evidence. See Comptroller’s Decision No. 102,695 (2010). In making the reasonable diligence determination, the Comptroller considers the following factors: the taxpayer’s audit history, the tax issues involved, whether a change in Comptroller policy occurred during the audit period, whether changes in the law took effect during the audit period, the size and sophistication of the taxpayer, whether tax was collected but not remitted, whether returns were timely filed, the completeness of the taxpayer’s records, the taxpayer’s efforts to comply with the recordkeeping requirements of this state, delinquencies in other taxes, reliance on advice provided by the Comptroller’s office, and the error rate in the current audit. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.5(b)(3), (d). To prevail, Petitioner must demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that penalty waiver is warranted. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 102,268 (2014). In this case, Petitioner had 20 late returns during the audit period, it did not provide business records for the audit, and the error rate remains over 78%. The ALJ finds that Petitioner failed to establish that penalty waiver was warranted.

Petitioner also contends interest waiver is warranted. Delinquent taxes draw interest beginning 60 days after the date due. Tex. Tax Code § 111.060(c). The Comptroller has discretionary authority to waive interest assessments and may exercise his discretion if interest was imposed as a result of undue delay caused by Comptroller personnel, reliance on advice provided by the Comptroller’s office, or natural disaster. Id. § 111.103; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.5(e). To prevail, Petitioner must demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that interest waiver is warranted. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e); see also Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,268 and 109,069 (2014). There is no evidence in the record to establish that interest waiver is warranted; therefore, that contention should be denied as well.

With respect to the 50% additional penalty, Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. Id. § 1.26(b)(1). Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed., 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

Gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, is sufficiently indicative of intent to evade the tax to warrant the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015). The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b).

In the instant matter, the underreporting identified by the audit constitutes gross error. See Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b). Gross underreporting of taxable sales, along with other factors or lack of a plausible explanation, is sufficiently indicative of intent to evade tax to warrant the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 105,232 (2012). In this case, Petitioner has not provided a plausible explanation for the gross underreporting. The ALJ concludes Staff’s evidence demonstrates that it is highly probable that the underreporting identified by the audit was the result of willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax.

In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011). The same principle applies to a limited liability company. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 112,305, 112,307, and 112,308 (2016). The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a). To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. Id. § 3.15(b). The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. Id. § 3.15(c). Petitioner offered no evidence to demonstrate that either the managing member of Petitioner, INDIVIDUAL A, or store manager INDIVIDUAL B was engaged in an independent course of conduct with regard to the fraudulent tax returns. The ALJ concludes the 50% additional penalty is warranted and should be sustained.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. ************** (Petitioner) operated two “drive-through” food and beverages stores, one in CITY, Texas (Outlet 1) and one in CITY, Texas (Outlet 2).

2. Petitioner’s sole managing member is INDIVIDUAL A.

3. The stores sold beer and wine, but did not sell distilled spirits and, therefore, did not hold a mixed beverage permit or remit mixed beverage gross receipts tax.

4. In 2019, the Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated an audit to verify Petitioner’s compliance with Texas sales and use tax laws in the period January 1, 2016, through December 31, 2019.

5. Petitioner did not respond to the auditor’s attempts at communication and did not provide business records for the audit.

6. Because Petitioner failed to provide adequate records, the audit was estimated using vendor-reported purchase data and the average sales prices at Petitioner’s outlets.

7. Due to the lack of business records, the auditor made observations at each outlet and recorded products sold, amount of the sales, and cash or credit sales during several hours at each location.

8. By documenting the food and alcohol sales, the auditor calculated a “product mix percentage” representing the ratio of beer sales to food sales. The product mix percentage for beer was 21.8% for Outlet 1 and 13.72% for Outlet 2.

9. The auditor obtained a beer price list during the observation and that list, along with the documentation of inventory purchases, allowed the audit to calculate a mark-up percentage of 44% for beer during the audit period.

10. For each outlet, the total estimated beer sales were calculated by multiplying beer purchases by the average markup percentage.

11. With estimated beer sales established, taxable sales for the audit period were calculated by dividing the total estimated beer sales by the product mix percentage. Petitioner’s reported taxable sales were then subtracted from the estimated taxable sales to arrive at the estimated additional taxable sales.

12. The additional tax due was calculated by multiplying the applicable state and local tax rates to the estimated additional taxable sales for each outlet.

13. On May 21, 2020, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing tax, 10% penalty, 50% additional penalty, and interest accrued to the account.

14. Petitioner requested a redetermination of the assessment, raising several contentions and providing additional documentation.

15. Staff agreed to adjust the assessment, and those adjustments are set out in Staff’s Exhibit 6.

16. The adjusted error rate is 78.44%.

17. Staff referred the above-referenced case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and on June 20, 2023, issued Petitioner a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. The notice contained a statement of the nature of the hearing; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing was to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaint or petition filed with the state agency.

18. On June 22, 2023, the Administrative Law Judge issued an order setting the written submission hearing.

19. The record closed August 28, 2023.

20. Petitioner did not submit evidence or argument for the written submission hearing.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over this matter. Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to this hearing, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearing. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. Sales tax is due on each sale of a taxable item in this state, and use tax is due on the storage, use or other consumption of a taxable item in Texas. Tex. Tax Code §§ 151.051, .101.

5. The term taxable item includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010.

6. The law requires retailers to keep records that reflect the total gross receipts from sales and the total purchases of taxable items. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

7. If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on any available information, including records of suppliers. Tex. Tax Code §§ 111.0042(d), .008(a).

8. Staff’s evidence is sufficient to establish, prima facie, that the estimated audit was authorized by statute and that the best information available was utilized.

9. It is Petitioner’s burden to show audit error by a preponderance of the evidence. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

10. Petitioner failed to demonstrate audit error, except as agreed by Staff.

11. Late penalties are automatically imposed on delinquent taxes. Tex. Tax Code § 111.061.

12. The Comptroller has the discretionary authority to waive late penalties if a taxpayer has exercised reasonable diligence to comply with tax laws. Tex. Tax Code § 111.103.

13. A taxpayer must establish reasonable diligence by a preponderance of evidence. See Comptroller’s Decision No. 102,695 (2010).

14. In making the reasonable diligence determination, the Comptroller considers the following factors: the taxpayer’s audit history, the tax issues involved, whether a change in Comptroller policy occurred during the audit period, whether changes in the law took effect during the audit period, the size and sophistication of the taxpayer, whether tax was collected but not remitted, whether returns were timely filed, the completeness of the taxpayer’s records, the taxpayer’s efforts to comply with the recordkeeping requirements of this state, delinquencies in other taxes, reliance on advice provided by the Comptroller’s office, and the error rate in the current audit. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.5(b)(3), (d).

15. To prevail, Petitioner must demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that penalty waiver is warranted. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 102,268 (2014).

16. Petitioner failed to establish that penalty waiver was warranted.

17. Delinquent taxes draw interest beginning 60 days after the date due. Tex. Tax Code § 111.060(c).

18. The Comptroller has discretionary authority to waive interest assessments and may exercise his discretion if interest was imposed as a result of undue delay caused by Comptroller personnel, reliance on advice provided by the Comptroller’s office, or natural disaster. Tex. Tax Code § 111.103; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.5(e).

19. To prevail, Petitioner must demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that interest waiver is warranted. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e); see also Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,268 and 109,069 (2014).

20. The ALJ finds interest waiver is not warranted.

21. Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax.

22. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(b)(1).

23. Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed., 2019); see also, Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

24. Gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, is sufficiently indicative of intent to evade the tax to warrant the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015).

25. The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b).

26. The underreporting identified by the audit constitutes gross error. See Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b).

27. Gross underreporting of taxable sales, along with other factors or lack of a plausible explanation, is sufficiently indicative of intent to evade tax to warrant the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 105,232 (2012).

28. Petitioner has not provided a plausible explanation for the underreporting.

29. Staff’s evidence demonstrates that it is highly probable that the underreporting identified by the audit was the result of willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax.

30. In the case of corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers or directors. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,756 (2011).

31. The same principle applies to a limited liability company. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 112,305, 112,307, and 112,308 (2016).

32. The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a).

33. To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(b).

34. The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. 34 Tex. Admin. Code. § 3.15(c).

35. Petitioner failed to demonstrate that either its managing member, INDIVIDUAL A, or store manager INDIVIDUAL B was engaged in an independent course of conduct with regard to the fraudulent tax returns.

36. The audit should be affirmed, except as agreed by Staff.

37. Staff’s evidence supports the application of the 50% additional penalty.
