Proposal For Decision

The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) audited ************** (Petitioner) for compliance with mixed beverage tax laws and made assessments for mixed beverage gross receipts tax (MBGRT), mixed beverage sales tax (MBST), 10% penalty, additional 50% penalty, and interest. Petitioner requested redetermination, asserting audit error and requesting waivers of the additional 50% penalty and interest. Staff amended the audit based on additional information and documentation provided. Staff then agreed to an adjustment to the units of beer sold in Exam 1H of each audit but contends that neither additional adjustments nor waivers of penalty or interest are warranted. In this Proposal for Decision (PFD), the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) finds that the proposed amended assessments should be upheld.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on June 6, 2023, ALJ Keneshia Washington issued the order setting the prehearing requirements and combining the cases for purposes of issuing a single PFD. The order was served on Petitioner using the same email address that Staff used to communicate with Petitioner’s representative during the administrative hearing process. On June 7, 2023, Staff issued Notices of Hearing to Petitioner. Eduardo Vasquez represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by INDIVIDUAL D, Petitioner’s managing member. The hearing convened via videoconference on August 23, 2023. A representative for Petitioner did not appear.[4] The record closed on the same day after Staff eFiled its exhibits admitted as evidence.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction in this proceeding. Therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE PRESENTED

Petitioner did not offer any exhibits or appear at the hearing. Staff presented the testimony of auditor, INDIVIDUAL A, and offered the following exhibits for each hearing:

1. Hearing Request Receipt;

2. Texas Notification of Audit Results;

3. Penalty & Interest Waiver;

4. Audit Report;

5. Audit Plan;

6. Amended Audit Report;

7. Amended Audit Plan;

8. Agreement to Purchase Nightclub;

9. Texas Franchise Tax Public Information Report 2019;

10. Certificate of Amendment 2017;

11. Agreement to Purchase Petitioner;

12. Petitioner Certificate of Formation;

13. Texas Franchise Tax Public Information Report 2014;

14. Texas Alcohol and Beverage Commission Mixed Beverage Permit Search;

15. Mixed Beverage Sales Tax Audit Trail Inquiry;

16. Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts Tax Audit Trail Inquiry;

17. Amended Exam 1H and Audit Adjustment Report;

18. Amended Exam 1B; and

19. Amended Exams 1A and 1.

B. STAFF AGREED ADJUSTMENTS

Staff agreed to an adjustment to the units of beer sold in Exam 1H of each audit as shown in its Exhibit 17 for each hearing.

C. MATERIAL FACTS AND ISSUES PRESENTED

During the period at issue, Petitioner held a mixed beverage permit and operated a bar in CITY, Texas. INDIVIDUAL B was a managing member of Petitioner and filed Petitioner’s monthly mixed beverage tax returns from February 2016 through August 2017.[5] In 2017, INDIVIDUAL D became Petitioner’s managing member, and INDIVIDUAL C filed Petitioner’s mixed beverage tax returns from October 2017 through September 2019.[6] Bar manager INDIVIDUAL E oversaw clearing the register, collecting the receipts at the end of the day, and keeping inventory records. INDIVIDUAL E or INDIVIDUAL D prepared Petitioner’s deposits.[7]

In December 2019, Staff initiated a mixed beverage tax compliance audit of Petitioner for the period February 1, 2016, through September 30, 2019. Petitioner provided the auditor with point-of-sale (POS) records for the periods December 2017 through October 2018 and February through September 2019.

The auditor initially performed a reconciliation of Petitioner’s mixed beverage sales as shown on the available POS reports and the amounts reported. The reconciliation revealed that Petitioner’s sales exceeded reported amounts for approximately 40% of the monthly periods during the audit, mostly from December 2017 through September 2019. The auditor conducted the audit by performing a depletion analysis based on the available monthly POS reports, a pour test, and vendor‑reported purchases. Using the serving sizes for distilled spirits, packaged beer, and draft beer as well as the vendor‑reported purchases, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and beer available for sale during the audit period. Petitioner had immaterial wine purchases and no wine sales during the audit period. The auditor then multiplied the average selling price based on the POS reports by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer. Petitioner did not provide documentation showing complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, or other potential allowances.

The difference between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts for distilled spirits and beer, resulting in a reporting error percentage of 120.54% for distilled spirits and 60.13% for beer. The auditor applied the underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from distilled spirits and beer sales for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts. The auditor added the reconciliation adjustments and then applied the respective tax rates to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due. The overall error rates for the assessments were approximately 70% for both MBST and MBGRT.

On April 30, 2020, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBGRT. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBST. Both assessments include tax, a 10% penalty, a 50% additional penalty, and accrued interest. Petitioner requested redetermination, contending the depletion analysis incorporated an incorrect average selling price for beer and erroneous services per container for distilled spirits. Petitioner also requested a waiver of the additional 50% penalty and interest. Petitioner provided additional documentation and information that supported adjustments. Staff amended the audit by adjusting the number of available beer bottles, the average selling price for beer, and the servings per container for beer used in the depletion analysis. Staff agreed to additional adjustments to the units of beer sold in Exam 1H of each audit as shown in its Exhibit 17 for each hearing. After the amendments and agreed adjustments, the overall error rates for the assessments remain at approximately 70% for both MBST and MBGRT. Staff did not agree to any additional adjustments or any waivers of penalty or interest and referred the matters to SOAH.

D. ALJ’S ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

A 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001. In addition, an 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002. As a mixed beverage permit holder, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4).

In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the MBGRT and MBST liabilities based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. Id. §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. Id. Thus, mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 115,139 and 115,140 (2019); Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017). The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011). Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation. See Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017) at 24.

In the present case, the proposed amended audit was based on a pour test at Petitioner’s establishment, available monthly POS reports, and vendor‑reported purchases. Thus, the ALJ finds that Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that the proposed amended audit was based on the best information available. The proposed amended audit was performed in accordance with established auditing procedures and is therefore entitled to a presumption of correctness. Comptroller’s Decision No. 110,206 (2018). Hence, Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to demonstrate that the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e).

Petitioner requested redetermination, contending the depletion analysis incorporated an incorrect average selling price for beer and erroneous services per container for distilled spirits. Petitioner provided additional documentation and information that supported adjustments. Staff amended the audit and then agreed to additional adjustments. Petitioner did not appear at the hearing or offer exhibits for the hearing.

Assertions in pleadings are insufficient to meet the burden of proof. See Comptroller’s Decision No. 105,892 (2012). Bare assertions are not a substitute for evidence and are insufficient to establish audit error. Comptroller’s Decision No. 115,999 (2020), citing to Baker v. Bullock, 529 S.W.2d 279 (Tex. Civ. App.— Austin 1975, writ ref’d n.r.e.); see also, Comptroller’s Decision No. 107,916 (2013). Petitioner has not provided any additional source records to controvert the depletion analysis or the overall results. Therefore, the ALJ finds that Petitioner failed to establish error in the proposed amended audit. The audit assessments should be upheld.

Petitioner requested waiver of interest and penalty. Delinquent taxes draw interest beginning 60 days after the date due. Tex. Tax Code § 111.060(c). The Comptroller has discretionary authority to waive interest assessments and may exercise his discretion if interest was imposed as a result of undue delay caused by Comptroller personnel, reliance on advice provided by the Comptroller’s office, or natural disaster. Id. § 111.103; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.5(e). To prevail, Petitioner must demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that interest waiver is warranted. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e); see also Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,268 and 109,069 (2014). Petitioner did not demonstrate any of the factors that may warrant interest waiver. The contention should be denied, and the interest applied should be upheld.

Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(b)(1). Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

The Comptroller has repeatedly held that, gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, sufficiently indicates intent to evade the tax and warrants the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015). The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b). The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019). Negligence, whether slight or great, is not the equivalent of fraud with intent to evade tax. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 45,514 (2006), 42,244 (2003), 38,886 (2002), 37,555 (1999), 35,527 (1997), 33,554 (1995); see also Webb v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 394 F.2d 366 (5th Cir. 1968).

In this case, the reconciliation revealed that Petitioner’s sales exceeded reported amounts for approximately 40% of the monthly periods during the audit, mostly from December 2017 through September 2019. After the amendments and agreed adjustments, the overall error rates for the assessments are approximately 70% for both MBST and MBGRT. Petitioner did not submit any evidence to support adjustments to the proposed amended assessments that would reduce the 70% error rate. Furthermore, Petitioner has not presented a plausible explanation for the underreporting. Therefore, the ALJ concludes Staff’s evidence is sufficient to support the application of the 50% penalty for each assessment.

With regard to corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors, or by its employees, and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers, directors, or employees. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 103,756 (2011); 102,200 (2010). The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a). To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. Id. § 3.15(b). The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. Id. § 3.15(c). The failure of INDIVIDUAL B, INDIVIDUAL C, and INDIVIDUAL D as managing members to accurately report Petitioner’s mixed beverage sales, MBGRT and MBST may be imputed to Petitioner. Therefore, the ALJ recommends affirming the 50% fraud penalty in the mixed beverage audit.

Petitioner presented documentation and an assertion that the business was sold. However, the assessments are not based on successor liability, so whether the business was sold has no bearing on the amount of the liability imposed on Petitioner. Furthermore, to the extent Petitioner’s representative and managing member, INDIVIDUAL D, seeks to argue that he is not personally liable for Petitioner’s MBGRT and MBST liabilities, the assessments at issue are not based on individual liability. Therefore, such an argument is not applicable.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. During the period at issue, ************** (Petitioner) held a mixed beverage permit and operated a bar in CITY, Texas.

2. Per Petitioner’s 2014 Texas Franchise Tax Public Information Report, INDIVIDUAL B was a managing member of Petitioner. INDIVIDUAL B filed Petitioner’s monthly mixed beverage tax returns from February 2016 through August 2017.

3. The company’s 2017 Certificate of Amendment for Entity Information and 2019 Texas Franchise Tax Public Information Report showed that INDIVIDUAL D became Petitioner’s managing member.

4. INDIVIDUAL C filed Petitioner’s mixed beverage tax returns from October 2017 through September 2019.

5. Bar manager INDIVIDUAL E oversaw clearing the register, collecting the receipts at the end of the day, and keeping inventory records.

6. INDIVIDUAL D or INDIVIDUAL E prepared Petitioner’s deposits.

7. In December 2019, the Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated a mixed beverage tax compliance audit of Petitioner for the period February 1, 2016, through September 30, 2019.

8. Petitioner provided the auditor with point-of-sale (POS) records for the periods December 2017 through October 2018 and February through September 2019.

9. The auditor initially performed a reconciliation of Petitioner’s mixed beverage sales as shown on the available POS reports and the amounts reported. The reconciliation revealed that Petitioner’s sales exceeded reported amounts for approximately 40% of the monthly periods during the audit, mostly from December 2017 through September 2019.

10. The auditor conducted the audit by performing a depletion analysis based on the available monthly POS reports, a pour test, and vendor‑reported purchases.

11. Using the serving sizes for distilled spirits, packaged beer, and draft beer as well as the vendor‑reported purchases, the auditor calculated the number of services of distilled spirits and beer available for sale during the audit period.

12. Petitioner had immaterial wine purchases and no wine sales during the audit period.

13. The auditor multiplied the average selling price based on the POS reports by the net services available to determine gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer.

14. Petitioner did not provide documentation showing complimentary drinks, opening and closing inventory, or other potential allowances.

15. The difference between the audited gross receipts and the reported gross receipts for distilled spirits and beer were divided by reported receipts for distilled spirits and beer, resulting in a reporting error percentage of 120.54% for distilled spirits and 60.13% for beer.

16. The auditor applied the underreporting error percentage to reported gross receipts from distilled spirits and beer sales for both assessments and allowed 5% for undocumented losses. The net result was scheduled as additional gross receipts.

17. The auditor added the reconciliation adjustments and then applied the respective tax rates to calculate the total additional MBGRT and MBST due.

18. The overall error rates for the assessments were approximately 70% for both MBST and MBGRT.

19. On April 30, 2020, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBGRT. On the same date, Staff issued a Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner assessing a liability for MBST. Both assessments included tax, a 10% penalty, a 50% additional penalty, and accrued interest.

20. Petitioner timely requested redetermination

21. Petitioner provided additional documentation and information that supported adjustments. Staff amended the audit by adjusting the number of available beer bottles, the average selling price for beer, and the servings per container for beer used in the depletion analysis. Staff agreed to additional adjustments to the units of beer sold in Exam 1H of each audit as shown in its Exhibit 17 for each hearing.

22. After the amendments and agreed adjustments, the overall error rates for the assessments remain at approximately 70% for both MBST and MBGRT.

23. Staff did not propose any additional adjustments or any waivers of penalty or interest.

24. Staff referred the above-referenced cases to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH)

25. On June 6, 2023, Administrative Law Judge Keneshia Washington issued the Order Consolidating Cases and Setting Prehearing Requirements, which included the pre-hearing requirements and instructions regarding access to the videoconference.

26. On June 7, 2023, Staff issued Petitioner Notices of Hearing. The notices contained a statement of the nature of the hearing; the date, time and location of the hearing; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing was to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaint or petition filed with the state agency.

27. The hearing convened on August 23, 2023.

28. Petitioner did not appear at the hearing or offer exhibits for the hearing.

29. The record closed on the same day after Staff eFiled its exhibits admitted as evidence.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over these matters. See Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to the hearing, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided a proper and timely notice of hearing. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. A 6.7% tax is imposed on the gross receipts from the sale, preparation, or service of mixed beverages or from the sale, preparation, or service of ice or nonalcoholic beverages that are sold, prepared, or served for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.021; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1001.

5. In addition, an 8.25% MBST is assessed on each mixed beverage sold, prepared, or served in this state and on ice and each nonalcoholic beverage sold, prepared, or served by a permittee in this state for the purpose of being mixed with an alcoholic beverage and consumed on the premises of the permittee. Tex. Tax Code § 183.041; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.1002.

6. As a mixed beverage permit holder, Petitioner was required to maintain records that reflected the purchases, sales, and gross receipts from the sale or service of alcoholic beverages. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 3.1001(j)‑(m), .1002(c)(4).

7. In examining the tax account of a permittee, the Comptroller may compute and determine the MBGRT and MBST liabilities based on reports filed with the Comptroller, records or information obtained from the permittee, records or information obtained from any seller who furnished alcoholic beverages to the permittee, or such other information that may come to the attention of the Comptroller. The Comptroller presumes that the disposition of all alcoholic beverages purchased by the permittee is taxable until established otherwise. 34 Tex. Admin Code §§ 3.1001(o)(1), .1002(c)(4).

8. Mixed beverage audits are generally completed by “depleting” a taxpayer’s alcoholic beverage purchases by the estimated number of services that a taxpayer had available for sale. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 115,139 and 115,140 (2019); Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017).

9. The depletion-analysis methodology is recognized and accepted by the Comptroller for auditing mixed beverage taxpayers. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 103,080 (2011).

10. Any audit adjustment resulting from a depletion analysis is considered an estimated audit due to the various components comprising the calculation. See Mixed Beverage Gross Receipts and Sales Tax Manual (2017) at 24.

11. Staff’s evidence demonstrates, prima facie, that the proposed amended audit was based on the best information available.

12. The proposed amended audit was performed in accordance with established auditing procedures and is therefore entitled to a presumption of correctness. Comptroller’s Decision No. 110,206 (2018).

13. Petitioner must produce contemporaneous records and supporting documentation to demonstrate that the tax amounts that Staff assessed are incorrect. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(a), (e).

14. Assertions in pleadings are insufficient to meet the burden of proof. See Comptroller’s Decision No. 105,892 (2012).

15. Bare assertions are not a substitute for evidence and are insufficient to establish audit error. Comptroller’s Decision No. 115,999 (2020), citing to Baker v. Bullock, 529 S.W.2d 279 (Tex. Civ. App.—Austin 1975, writ ref’d n.r.e.); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 107,916 (2013).

16. Petitioner failed to establish error in the proposed amended audit.

17. The audit assessments should be upheld.

18. Delinquent taxes draw interest beginning 60 days after the date due. Tex. Tax Code § 111.060(c).

19. The Comptroller has discretionary authority to waive interest assessments and may exercise his discretion if interest was imposed as a result of undue delay caused by Comptroller personnel, reliance on advice provided by the Comptroller’s office, or natural disaster. Tex. Tax Code § 111.103; 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.5(e).

20. To prevail, Petitioner must demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that interest waiver is warranted. See 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e); see also Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,268 and 109,069 (2014).

21. The interest applied should be upheld.

22. Texas Tax Code § 111.061(b) authorizes a 50% penalty when the failure to pay the tax or file a report when due is the result of fraud or intent to evade the tax.

23. Staff bears the burden to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the imposition of additional penalty for willful or fraudulent failure to pay tax is warranted. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(b)(1).

24. Clear and convincing evidence is evidence demonstrating that the thing to be proved is highly probable. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019); see also Comptroller’s Decision No. 101,773 (2011).

25. The Comptroller has repeatedly held that, gross underreporting, along with other factors or no plausible explanation, sufficiently indicates intent to evade the tax and warrants the assessment of the fraud penalty. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision No. 111,804 (2015).

26. The Tax Code defines gross error to mean that, after correction of the error, the amount due and payable exceeds the amount initially reported by at least 25%. Tex. Tax Code § 111.205(b).

27. The term “plausible” is defined as conceivably true or successful; possibly correct or even likely; reasonable; and reasonably convincing and seemingly truthful, though possibly mendacious. See Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019).

28. Negligence, whether slight or great, is not the equivalent of fraud with intent to evade tax. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 45,514 (2006), 42,244 (2003), 38,886 (2002), 37,555 (1999), 35,527 (1997), 33,554 (1995); see also Webb v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 394 F.2d 366 (5th Cir. 1968).

29. Staff’s evidence is sufficient to support the application of the 50% penalty for each assessment.

30. With regard to corporate taxpayers, the Comptroller recognizes that a corporation is a separate legal entity that is controlled by its officers and directors, or by its employees, and that the requisite intent of a corporation is determined from the actions of the officers, directors, or employees. See Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 103,756 (2011); 102,200 (2010).

31. The Comptroller may impute to the taxpayer the acts or omissions of: (1) any officer, director, manager, or governing authority of the taxpayer; and (2) any agent or employee with the actual or apparent authority to prepare information for or submit information to the comptroller. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(a).

32. To avoid imputing the acts or omissions of a person to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may present evidence that the person was engaged in an independent course of conduct that did not further any purpose of the taxpayer. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(b).

33. The Comptroller may impose the additional penalty on the taxpayer without regard to whether an officer, manager, director, partner, or other person is personally liable for fraudulent tax evasion under the Tax Code. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.15(c).

34. The failure of INDIVIDUAL B, INDIVIDUAL C, and INDIVIDUAL D as a managing member to accurately report Petitioner’s mixed beverage sales, MBGRT and MBST may be imputed to Petitioner.

35. The 50% fraud penalty should be affirmed for both assessments.
